reason: The Commission's 2023 analytical report found that the law on access to the labour market made no difference between EU workers and other third-country nationals, and the 2024 report recorded amendments letting EU citizens work without a work permit. The 2025 report recorded a law of July 2025 giving EU citizens a separate regime, and the 2026 report the entry into force in March 2026 of the law on free movement and residence of EU citizens, aimed at alignment; the improvement is legal only. The chapter rating (early stage in 2023 and 2024, some level in 2025, between some and moderate in 2026) covers the whole chapter and was used as context only.

Law No. 200/2025, in force since March 2026, gives EU citizens a regime separate from other foreigners and, by the government's account, equal treatment with nationals, but the 2026 key recommendation still asks for continued alignment on access to the labour market and equal treatment of EU workers. The amendments to the employment law and its implementing decision, the adjustment of secondary legislation by several ministries and the removal of the citizenship condition for staff of private employment agencies are still at draft or planning stage. What remains is secondary and sectoral legislation giving EU workers equal access to employment services, active measures, service housing and private placement, and its application in practice.

Access for EU citizens to the labour market and equal treatment are central to the chapter and are named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, but not in those of 2023 or 2024, so the test of three or more reports is not met. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found among the 47 Moldova items on it; if the reviewers count the 2023 report's general call to align legislation with the acquis as the same recommendation, this would be High.

The remaining work is national legislation and staff training led by the Ministry of Labour and other ministries, and the drafts are already prepared and under consultation. Past progress is clear: the Commission reports amendments in force from January 2024 and Law No. 200/2025 in force from March 2026.

In 2023 the Commission found that EU citizens needed a temporary residence permit for work and that their family members were treated as other foreigners, while the 2023 report recorded amendments easing temporary residence for EU citizens; the 2024 report recorded amendments in force from January 2024 letting them work without a work permit. The 2025 report recorded a separate regime for EU citizens, and the 2026 report the entry into force of the free movement law in March 2026 and a standard operating procedure for their residence documents; the improvement is mainly legal. The chapter rating covers the whole chapter and was used as context only.

Under Law No. 200/2025 EU citizens need no work authorisation and, for stays over 90 days, a residence card not tied to a purpose, but the Commission reports that only 28 applications for the new residence documents had been submitted after the March 2026 procedure, while 422 EU citizens were still to be documented under the old stay-for-work regime in 2025. Full separation of the two regimes in the general law on foreigners depends on a draft law due to apply from 1 June 2027, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs' secondary legislation on registering EU citizens is still being revised. What remains is the practical move of EU citizens and their family members to the new residence cards and the completion of the implementing rules.

Work permits and residence conditions for EU workers are central to the chapter, but they are not named separately in a key recommendation; the 2025 and 2026 key recommendations on access for EU citizens to the labour market can be read as covering them, which would still make only two reports. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found among the 59 Moldova items on it.

The legal change has been made and the General Inspectorate for Migration has an operating procedure, so what is left is mostly administrative and within national control. Few EU citizens had applied for the new documents by 2026, and full separation of the regimes depends on a new foreigners law that is still a draft, so progress depends on the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Inspectorate following through.

The issue is first raised in the Commission's 2025 key recommendation to reinforce the employment service's IT infrastructure for EURES, when the 2025 report also recorded a new EURES department with a designated officer from January 2025. The 2026 report records technical standards for matching vacancies and CVs with the EURES portal and a new integrated information system developed in December 2025, aiming at fully digitalised services by 2027, while widening the recommendation to systems for EESSI and the EHIC. The chapter rating was not decisive, as the issue is only part of the chapter.

The employment agency has a Labour Migration and EURES directorate (five of six posts filled) and technical standards for exchange with the EURES portal, but the interoperability of its information system with EURES, staff training on EURES and the rules on personal data in that exchange are still planned. The agency's own reports for 2024 and 2025 say it lacks a modern information system, and the new system, funded through the EU Delegation, is still being developed. What remains is a working connection between the agency's information system and the EURES platform, operated by trained staff, before accession.

The employment service's IT capacity for EURES is named in the key recommendations of the 2025 and 2026 reports, two reports, and supports a chapter requirement that applies from accession. No benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found among the 32 Moldova items on it.

The work sits mainly with one agency, which has already set up a EURES directorate and technical standards, so there is evidence of past progress. The new information system depends on external funding and on technical connection work that is still planned, and the agency reports unfilled posts within its staff ceiling.

The issue is not raised in EU material: the two Commission items are counts of residence permits for 2023 and 2025, so the standard scale was not decisive and the judgement rests on the issue's own items. These describe the same barriers from 2024 to 2026: the migration inspectorate's 2024 proposals to remove problems found in the foreigners law, a 2025 study finding the procedure for employing foreigners bureaucratic, and UNHCR's 2026 finding that only 29 percent of working-age Ukrainian refugees are in paid work, with language, recognition of qualifications and childcare as barriers. The new law on admission of foreigners that would change the rules is a draft due to apply from June 2027.

There is no EU requirement on this issue, so the gap is judged on the issue's own items. The draft law on admission of foreigners and the draft amendment extending employment services to more categories of foreigners are proposals, and consultation comments on the draft law point to work permits tied to one employer and no clear separation between labour inspection and immigration control, while refugees still face language, recognition and childcare barriers. What remains is a law in force that eases third-country workers' access to the labour market and protects their rights after admission, and support that reaches refugees in practice.

The issue is not raised in EU material, which only counts residence permits, and this keeps priority from being High; no Commission recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under it was found among the 193 Moldova items on it. The evidence comes from national, international organisation and research sources, which do not raise priority.

A full draft law on admission of foreigners and a draft amendment to the employment law have been prepared and consulted, and the employment agency already supports refugees with partner organisations. Against that, the barriers named by UNHCR (language, recognition of diplomas, childcare) need several ministries and funding, and the draft law would apply only from June 2027.

Only two Moldova items fall under this issue: a 2021 Commission finding on use of the online tender platform for COVID-19 procurement and a 2023 report of a regulation requiring most low-value procurement to go through the State Registry of Public Procurement system. Neither states that modules are incomplete or underused, so no sequence can be drawn, and the chapter rating was not used.

No item among the two Moldova items on this issue states an EU requirement on incomplete or underused e-procurement modules or on use of procurement data for red-flag analysis, and the use of the low-value procurement module required by the 2023 regulation is not reported. What remains is not known from the evidence held.

No Commission recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found among the two Moldova items on it, and the 2021 finding concerns the transparency of emergency procurement rather than the electronic tools themselves.
The two items on this issue say nothing about the actors, costs or obstacles involved in fuller use of the e-procurement modules, so tractability cannot be judged.

The only Commission items are two 2023 calls, in the analytical report and the 2023 report, for electronic platforms and procedures alongside legal alignment on professional qualifications, and no item among the seven Moldova items on this issue gives a later EU assessment. The government's 2025 plans to reconfigure the public services portal as the point of single contact and to link the National Register of Qualifications with Europass are proposals, so there is no sequence to judge.

The 2023 Commission calls for electronic platforms and procedures are met so far only by plans: reconfiguring the public services portal as the point of single contact and making the National Register of Qualifications interoperable with Europass are both proposed. What remains is a point of single contact giving service providers full online information and procedures, and an electronic register of regulated professions and qualifications.

The Commission's calls for electronic platforms in this area appear only in 2023, as part of wider recommendations on professional qualifications, and their link to the theme is doubtful; no key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found among the seven Moldova items on it.

The public services portal already works and could be reconfigured, and the work lies with national bodies. Against that, both measures are only proposed, the government expects possible problems of interoperability with EU platforms, and there is no evidence of past progress on them.

In 2023 the Commission reported that 67.5% of households had internet at home (58% in rural areas), in 2025 that high-speed broadband reached 57% of the population by mid-2024 while regional disparities persisted, and in 2026 that nearly 95% of households had internet access. The 2026 sub-area wording on 5G deployment, which matches this part of the issue, is some progress, with coverage of 25 to 35%; the Chapter 10 rating was used as context only, as the issue is part of the chapter.

Coverage and take-up have risen, and the Commission's assessment for the third Reform and Growth Facility release records 6.9% more fixed-broadband connections and faster speeds between 2025 and 2026, but 5G coverage remains well below the EU average and the Reform Agenda describes a rural-urban digital divide. The government counts 431 localities in white areas without fixed broadband, and the plan to develop networks there is proposed and waits for the regulator's geographic survey. What remains is high-capacity fixed and 5G coverage in rural and small localities.

The rural-urban digital divide is named in a 2024 economic key recommendation on infrastructure investment, the Reform Agenda describes it and the 2026 report rates 5G deployment, but no Chapter 10 key recommendation, benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition on coverage was found among the 143 Moldova items on this issue. The related Reform Agenda step concerns alignment with the Electronic Communications Code, which belongs to another issue.

Spectrum was awarded through competitions in 2024 and 2025, operators are investing and the Commission records progress on 5G, which is evidence of past progress. Closing the remaining gaps depends on private operators and on public funding for small, isolated localities, which the government says require significant investment.

In 2021 the draft data protection law had been awaiting second reading since 2018, and in 2023 the Commission found the law only to some extent aligned with the GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive. The 2024 report recorded adoption of the GDPR law, the 2025 report its entry into force due in August 2026, and the 2026 report its entry into force, the adoption in August 2026 of a law aligning with the Law Enforcement Directive and ratification of the second protocol to Convention 108; the improvement is legal only. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue spans several chapters.

The main laws the Commission has called for since 2023 are now adopted, but the 2026 report says Moldova should still implement EU standards on contractual clauses between operators and processors, and the 2026 key recommendation still asks for further alignment with EU data protection standards. The draft order on standard contractual clauses is only proposed, and harmonisation of sector laws, pending since 2020 according to the 2023 report, is not reported as complete. What remains is the rules on standard contractual clauses and the harmonisation of sector laws with the new data protection laws.

Alignment of data protection legislation is named in the Chapter 10 key recommendations of the 2024, 2025 and 2026 reports, after the 2023 report called for the data protection law to be amended, and it is central to the data theme. No Reform Agenda payment condition under this issue was found among the 83 Moldova items on it.

Moldova adopted the GDPR law in 2024 and, in 2026, the law enforcement data protection law and the ratification of the Convention 108 protocol, which is strong evidence of past progress. What is left is mainly an order on contractual clauses, already drafted, which the government controls.

No item among the 22 Moldova items on this issue is a Commission finding or recommendation on the framework's alignment; the EU items are a Growth Plan support measure and a 2026 note that the open data law is in line with the European Interoperability Framework. The government stated in 2025 that the national framework follows the Framework's principles but that the Interoperable Europe Act is not transposed, and drafting of the amending law was announced in February 2026, which is too short a record to show a direction.

By the government's own account the Interoperable Europe Act has not been transposed, and the law amending Law No. 142/2018 to do so was only initiated in February 2026; the Interoperable Europe factsheet notes that Moldova is not yet part of the European Interoperability Framework data collection. What remains is transposition of the Interoperable Europe Act into the data exchange and interoperability law and alignment of the national framework with the latest European Interoperability Framework.

The issue is not raised as a requirement in the Commission's reports or the Reform Agenda; no such item was found among the 22 Moldova items on it, which keeps priority from being High. It rests on the government's own gap analysis and an EU support measure under the Growth Plan.

The change is one amendment to an existing law, prepared by the government, and Moldova already has a working legal and technical interoperability framework. Drafting began only in February 2026, so there is no evidence yet of progress on transposing the Act itself.

The Commission reported in 2023 that data exchange through MConnect let the electoral commission check party financing more effectively, but in 2025 it said interoperability between automated verification systems and state registries must still be strengthened, and in 2026 it noted constraints on the full practical functioning of interoperable verification tools. Other sources show connections growing (336 institutions in 2023 according to SIGMA) while the same underuse is reported: the World Bank in 2024 found interoperability yet to be streamlined, the government in 2025 found systems fragmented, and the data protection authority in 2026 found state bodies still using COI access outside the platform. The Chapter 10 rating was not decisive, as the issue is cross-cutting.

The platform and the legal duty to exchange data through it are in place, with sanctions since 2021, and SIGMA found the base registers connected to it in 2023. The data protection authority finds that state bodies still access personal data through COI technology outside the platform, which conflicts with the government's statement that data exchange takes place exclusively through MConnect, and the Commission in 2026 still finds the interoperable verification tools for asset declarations not fully functioning. What remains is regular use of the platform by all institutions, including an end to access outside it, and full data exchange for asset declaration checks.

Interoperability for asset declaration checks is part of a Reform Agenda step (all declarations through the new e-Integrity system, with interoperability ensured through MConnect), is named in the 2025 main findings on Chapter 23 and is repeated as a finding in 2026, and regular use of the platform is central to the interoperability theme. The EU items concern only asset declaration checks; if the reviewers read the Reform Agenda step as concerning the e-Integrity system rather than this issue, this would be Medium.

The platform, the law and sanctions already exist and connections have grown, which is evidence of past progress. Against that, the remaining problem lies with many institutions that the World Bank says work in silos, and the data protection authority reports that bodies notified repeatedly have still not moved to the platform.

The Commission found in 2025 that Moldova was not yet fully aligned with the Chips Act and in 2026 that it was yet to align with it. The 2026 sub-area wording on semiconductors, which matches this issue, is some progress, but it rests on the April 2026 law on topographies of semiconductor products, an intellectual property matter outside the issue, so alignment with the Chips Act has not moved.

The 2026 key recommendation asks for further alignment with the semiconductor acquis, and the government plans to transpose the Chips Act by the end of 2026 but states that there are no national rules on semiconductor production facilities and no responsible institution. What remains is transposition of the Chips Act and the designation and staffing of a competent authority.

Alignment with the semiconductor acquis is a key recommendation in the 2026 report, following a 2025 finding, but only in one report, and no benchmark or Reform Agenda payment condition under it was found among the 14 Moldova items on it. The government describes the sector in Moldova as almost non-existent, which makes the issue less central to the theme.

The government reports that no institution is responsible for the area, that no ministry employee covers it and that a new post is needed, and the sector is at an early stage. Transposition is planned for the end of 2026, but there is no evidence of past progress on the Chips Act itself.
